caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:000785

inputs.what: Method details read from the paper's code (normalization parameters in config/preprocess.yml, the skipping of planes without red cells and the trial segmentation in src/nwb_processor.py, the tracked-neuron criteria); no data, labels or values were taken from it.

attempts.entry_title: Projection-specific routing of odor information in the olfactory cortex (Daste, Pierré et al. 2025)
attempts.summary: The paper's results on response timing and odor identity coding in piriform neurons projecting to the olfactory bulb (OB-p) or mPFC (mPFC-p) mostly held up in this data, while most valence and concentration decoding results did not, and the projection classifiers could not be tested. OB-p neurons responded more often and earlier and decoded identity earlier, though in the fast imaging data projection is confounded with mouse. mPFC-p populations decoded concentration further above chance than reported, OB-p populations still encoded valence late in the task, and performance gains across days were not significant. The transformer and MLP classifiers need hyperparameter tables missing from the preprint. Correct-trial valence decoding was blocked because the paper's trial construction cannot be identified.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Daste, Pierré et al. (2025) on dandiset 000785, which holds two-photon imaging of OB-projecting and mPFC-projecting neurons in anterior piriform cortex during passive odor exposure (identity, concentration and 30 Hz experiments) and Go/NoGo learning, with cells tracked across sessions. It covers the neuron counts, single-cell response properties, odor identity and concentration decoding, behavior, valence decoding and the tracked-neuron analyses. The transformer and MLP classifiers are not run, as their hyperparameters are missing from the paper's text.

notebooks.title: Daste, Pierré et al. (2025), passive odor experiments, from dandiset 000785
Daste, Pierré et al. (2025), Go/NoGo experiment, from dandiset 000785

outcomes.statement: The passive identity dataset holds 81 OB-p, 84 mPFC-p and 1978 untagged neurons from 10 mice; the concentration dataset 87 OB-p, 102 mPFC-p and 2232 untagged neurons from 10 mice; the Go/NoGo dataset 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p tagged) with, per session, 95 +/- 2 OB-p, 87 +/- 8 mPFC-p and 1690 +/- 35 untagged neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Calcium imaging of piriform neurons with distinct projection targets, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: head-fixed mice were either exposed to 8 monomolecular odorants at a single concentration (10 mice, totaling 81 OB-p, 84 mPFC-p, and 1978 untagged aPCx neurons ... or to three odorants at three concentrations each (10 mice, totaling 87 OB-p, 102 mPFC-p, and 2232 untagged cells ... Per session (mean ± SD), we recorded 95 ± 2 OB-p, 87 ± 8 mPFC-p, and 1690 ± 35 untagged neurons
outcomes.notes: With the code's rule (planes without a red cell skipped), identity has 81 OB-p, 84 mPFC-p and 1937 untagged neurons from 10 mice and concentration 87, 102 and 2132 from 10 mice, all within tolerance; over all planes the identity untagged count is 2328. The Go/NoGo per-session OB-p mean is 103.3 (days 1 to 3, reading a) or 107.5 (days 0 to 3, reading b), outside 95 +/- 2 under every reading. The mPFC-p mean is 91.7 (a) and 94.5 (b) without sub-668, within 87 +/- 8, and 95.7 and 98.2 with it. The untagged mean is 1623.3 (a) and 1656.2 (b) without sub-668, 1655.0 and 1690.0 with it; 1623.3 is outside 1690 +/- 35, the other three within. Measured values are the code rule and reading (a) without sub-668.
deviations: Counts follow the code's compute_dFF0, which skips planes without red cells (src/nwb_processor.py at commit f478b34).

The paper's Go/NoGo experiment has 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p); the dandiset has 8. The analysis leaves out sub-668, an assumption: it is the only Go/NoGo mouse without tracking identifiers and has 24 to 58 cells per session against 98 to 361 for the others. Its day 3 performance (90%) passes the Methods' 60% exclusion threshold, so the paper's stated rule does not exclude it.

outcomes.statement: The 30 Hz subset holds 24 OB-p, 27 mPFC-p and 424 untagged neurons from 5 mice.
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: in a subset of experiments (5 mice, totaling 24 OB-p, 27 mPFC-p, and 424 untagged cells), we examined the temporal structure of odor responses by performing high-speed (30 Hz) imaging
outcomes.notes: 24 OB-p, 27 mPFC-p and 424 untagged neurons from 5 mice, exactly the paper's counts.

outcomes.statement: OB-p and mPFC-p mice do not differ in the number of jGCaMP7f neurons or of co- labeled jGCaMP7f/tdTomato neurons.
outcomes.source: Figure S2B legend
outcomes.quote: Quantification of jGCaMP7f and co-labeled jGCaMP7f/tdTomato-expressing neurons in OB-p and mPFC-p mice. (OB-p, N = 9; mPFC-p, N = 10. Unpaired two-tailed t-test
outcomes.notes: No unpaired t-test has p < 0.05 under any reading: jGCaMP7f neurons p = 0.187 (first session) and 0.373 (mean over sessions); co-labeled count p = 0.585 and 0.985; co-labeled percentage p = 0.427 and 0.702. The dandiset has 10 OB-p and 8 mPFC-p mice, where the legend has 9 and 10.
deviations: Suite2p cells over all planes count as jGCaMP7f neurons and finalized red cells as co-labeled; the legend's counts may come from histology or another selection.
10 OB-p and 8 mPFC-p mice in place of 9 and 10.

outcomes.statement: An MLP trained on normalized fluorescence traces pooled across the identity and Go/NoGo datasets classifies OB-p against mPFC-p neurons with F1 scores of 0.688 (OB-p) and 0.557 (mPFC-p).
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal structure of activity predicts OB-p vs mPFC-p identity, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: The MLP achieved F1 scores of 0.688 (OB-p) and 0.557 (mPFC-p)
outcomes.notes: Not run. Tables 5 (transformer hyperparameters), 6 (held-out animal pairs) and 8 (final MLP hyperparameters) are missing from the paper's text, and the paper's code at commit f478b34 holds only an SVM demo for projection decoding; the figure code is to be released on publication. The criterion blocks the claim until Table 8 is supplied.

outcomes.statement: A transformer classifier on single-neuron calcium traces decodes projection target with F1 0.759 (OB-p) and 0.744 (mPFC-p) when neurons from all animals are split, and 0.754 (OB-p) and 0.623 (mPFC-p) when one OB-p and one mPFC-p animal are held out.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal structure of activity predicts OB-p vs mPFC-p identity, paragraph 1; Figure S3B
outcomes.quote: which improved test performance to 0.759 (OB-p) and 0.744 (mPFC-p) ( Figure S3B ) ... Performance remained high ... 0.754 OB-p; 0.623 mPFC-p
outcomes.notes: Not run. Tables 5 (transformer hyperparameters), 6 (held-out animal pairs) and 8 (final MLP hyperparameters) are missing from the paper's text, and the paper's code at commit f478b34 holds only an SVM demo for projection decoding; the figure code is to be released on publication. The criterion blocks the claim until Tables 5 and 6 are supplied.

outcomes.statement: Attention rollout on correctly classified neurons puts the informative epochs early after odor onset (about 0 to 3 s) for OB-p neurons and later in the trial for mPFC-p neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal structure of activity predicts OB-p vs mPFC-p identity, paragraph 2; Figure 1G and Figure S3D
outcomes.quote: informative epochs cluster early after odor onset (around 0-3 s) for OB-p neurons, but later in the trial for mPFC-p neurons
outcomes.notes: Depends on transformer-projection-f1, blocked for the missing Table 5.

outcomes.statement: The transformer's penultimate-layer embeddings separate OB-p from mPFC-p neurons, with little clustering by animal or dataset.
outcomes.source: Results, Temporal structure of activity predicts OB-p vs mPFC-p identity, paragraph 2; Figure 1F and Figure S3E to S3G
outcomes.quote: which separated OB-p and mPFC-p well with minimal clustering by animal or dataset
outcomes.notes: Depends on transformer-projection-f1, blocked for the missing Table 5.

outcomes.statement: Lifetime sparseness does not differ significantly between OB-p, mPFC-p and untagged neurons in the identity dataset.
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure 2B
outcomes.quote: Odor responses in PCx were generally sparse on the single cell level, with no significant differences in lifetime sparseness between groups
outcomes.notes: The data do not settle the outcome. With neurons never active on an odor trial left out (21 OB-p, 11 mPFC-p and 230 untagged under the start reading), mPFC-p and untagged neurons differ: medians 0.774 and 0.714, Bonferroni p = 0.0067 (start reading of the binarization window) and 0.015 (centre reading); OB-p against mPFC-p (corrected p = 1.0) and OB-p against untagged (0.38 and 0.42) do not differ. Kept with sparseness set to 0, no pair differs (smallest corrected p 0.061 start, 0.10 centre), which would reproduce the claim; set to 1, OB-p and mPFC-p each differ from untagged (corrected p 0.0079 and 0.019 start, 0.011 and 0.040 centre). The paper's formula and its handling of an all-zero response are lost from the text, so none of the three treatments has a basis in the paper, and the two that keep every neuron give opposite outcomes. The criterion's n (81, 84, 1978) is also the n of Figures 2C and 2E, so it may be the group sizes and not evidence that never-active neurons were kept in 2B. Blocked as methods_underspecified after the third verification round; the first record gave not reproduced with never-active neurons left out.
deviations: Neurons never active on an odor trial have no defined sparseness and are left out (21 OB-p, 11 mPFC-p and 230 untagged under the start reading), an assumption. The paper's formula is lost from the text and it does not say how such neurons were treated; leaving out an undefined value is the standard treatment, as in figs10e-sparseness-slope-no-difference. The Figure 2B legend's n (81, 84, 1978) counts every neuron, which may mean they were kept with some value; both fills are shown, and they give different outcomes. The question is recorded for the paper's authors.
Untagged neurons are those of planes with red cells (1937, against the paper's 1978).

outcomes.statement: Mutual information between binarized activity and odor identity does not differ between OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, but is lower for OB-p than untagged neurons (p = 0.012).
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: Mutual information did not differ significantly between projection sub-populations, but was lower for OB-p neurons than for untagged neurons (p = 0.012)

statistics.test: not named; two-sided Mann-Whitney U with Bonferroni correction is the test of the other Figure 2 comparisons

outcomes.notes: OB-p and mPFC-p do not differ (corrected p = 1.0), as the paper says, but OB-p is not significantly lower than untagged: medians 0.069 and 0.079 bits, corrected p = 0.19 (start) and 0.17 (centre), against the paper's 0.012.
deviations: Mutual information from empirical frequencies in bits (claims file reading; the formula is lost from the text).

outcomes.statement: Population sparseness per trial differs only between OB-p and untagged populations (p = 1.26 x 10^-5).
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: At the ensemble level, population sparseness differed only between OB-p ensembles and the untagged populations

statistics.test: not named; two-sided Mann-Whitney U with Bonferroni correction presumed

outcomes.notes: All three pairs differ, not only OB-p against untagged: OB-p against mPFC-p corrected p = 8.7e-06 (start) and 4.7e-05 (centre), OB-p against untagged 1e-07 and 2e-06, mPFC-p against untagged below 1e-07. OB-p population sparseness (median 0.925) lies between untagged (0.886) and mPFC-p (0.952). With binary activity, population sparseness is a function of the fraction of active cells and the group size, so this test repeats the proportion-responding comparison.

outcomes.statement: A higher proportion of OB-p than mPFC-p neurons responds to odorants.
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: with OB-p neurons responding in a significantly higher proportion than mPFC-p neurons (two-sided Mann–Whitney U test with Bonferroni corrected p-values, p = 5.79 × 10⁻ 7 )
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), per pseudo-population trial: 9.49% of OB-p and 6.94% of mPFC-p neurons active on average, corrected p = 9e-06 (start) and 4.7e-05 (centre). Reading (b), per neuron: not significant (corrected p = 1.0). The paper's p = 5.79e-07 is not matched in size.

outcomes.statement: OB-p populations contain higher fractions of both unreliable and reliable responsive cells per trial (10.97% and 1.54%) than mPFC-p populations (8.71% and 0.25%).
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 2; Figure 2E
outcomes.quote: OB-p populations contained higher fractions of both unreliable and reliable cells (10.97% and 1.54%, respectively) than mPFC-p populations ( Figure 2E , 8.71% and 0.25%
outcomes.notes: With Bonferroni over the 3 group pairs, both tests hold under no combination of the 16 readings: OB-p has more reliable responsive cells per trial than mPFC-p under all of them (corrected p <= 0.0003), but not more unreliable ones (smallest corrected p = 0.063, under b, c, e, h). At most one of the four percentages is within tolerance under any combination (for example a, c, f, g gives OB-p 7.64% unreliable and 16.20% reliable, mPFC-p 8.69% and 12.02%). With Bonferroni over the 2 tests, both tests hold under b, c, e, h (unreliable 17.23% against 15.93%, raw p = 0.0211, corrected 0.042), with no value within tolerance, which would make the claim partially reproduced. Bonferroni over the 2 tests is a reading this attempt added, not one the criterion names. The question of the correction is recorded as a finding for the paper's authors.
deviations: The number of comparisons in the Bonferroni correction is not stated for Figure 2E. Assumed 3, the pairs of the panel's three groups, as for the other Figure 2 comparisons (for example the latencies of Figure 2F); Bonferroni over the 2 tests is shown and gives a different outcome.

The reliability rule (a cell responds when its mean 0 to 5 s exceeds the baseline mean plus 2.33 SD) is from the Methods; its baseline window, per-trial or pooled baseline, and the 'more than half' denominator are the claims file's readings.

outcomes.statement: In the 30 Hz data OB-p neurons reach their first calcium peak after odor onset sooner than mPFC-p neurons; OB-p and untagged neurons do not differ.
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 3; Figure 2F
outcomes.quote: OB-p neurons exhibited shorter latencies to reach the first peak of calcium activity following odor onset compared to mPFC-p neurons
outcomes.notes: Per trial (a): median latency 3.58 s for OB-p and 4.65 s for mPFC-p, corrected p = 3.1e-16; OB-p against untagged (3.61 s) corrected p = 1.0; mPFC-p against untagged 2.7e-22. Per neuron (b): 3.84 against 4.62 s, corrected p = 0.030. By mouse the OB-p medians are 2.70 to 4.96 s and the mPFC-p medians 4.59 to 4.79 s. The odor onset (stim_onset_timestamp) falls 1 to 10 ms after a rising edge of the files' sniff signal (acquisition/sniff_on) in all 500 trials, so latencies are measured from a sniff-aligned onset, as the paper describes. Projection is confounded with mouse: sub-2456 and sub-2457 are the only mPFC mice of this dataset, and their untagged neurons are slow too (medians 4.82 and 4.12 s, against 2.70 to 3.73 s in the OB mice). Within each mouse OB-p is not faster than untagged (2.70 against 2.70 s, p = 0.55; 3.51 against 2.97 s, p = 0.00034; 4.96 against 3.73 s, p = 8e-16), and mPFC-p is as slow as its own mouse's untagged neurons or slower (4.59 against 4.82 s, p = 0.46; 4.79 against 4.12 s, p = 0.00065). The criterion pools neurons, so the outcome stands, but the latency difference follows the mouse at least as much as the projection. These two mice also supply 61 of the 93 day 3 Go/NoGo mPFC-p cells.
deviations: The first second of each trial is left out by starting the trace 4 s before onset; the trace ends 15 s after onset, more than a second before the trial's end.

outcomes.statement: OB-p neurons have more calcium peaks at early time points after odor onset than mPFC-p neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 3; Figure 2G and Figure S4A to S4C
outcomes.quote: OB-p neurons also had more peaks during earlier time points than mPFC-p neurons
outcomes.notes: Mean peaks per trial per neuron, 0 to 2 s: OB-p 0.198, mPFC-p 0.138 (Mann-Whitney p = 0.17); 0 to 3 s: 0.349 and 0.203 (p = 0.026). One of the three OB-p mice (sub-2401) has fewer early peaks (0.073 and 0.122) than either mPFC-p mouse. The groups are confounded with mouse, as for the latencies; in 0 to 3 s the untagged neurons of the two mPFC mice also have few early peaks (0.216 and 0.302), against 0.464 and 0.491 in sub-2372 and sub-2400 and 0.307 in sub-2401. The OASIS variant (Figure S4) was not run.

outcomes.statement: Odor identity decoded from 5 s windows reaches similar accuracy in size-matched OB- p and mPFC-p pseudo-populations, above chance and slightly below untagged.
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 4; Figure 2H
outcomes.quote: both OB-p and mPFC-p pseudo-populations reached similar accuracy levels, significantly above chance but slightly lower than the untagged population ( Figure 2H ; two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.398)
outcomes.notes: The two windows disagree. With 0 to 5 s (legend) OB-p and mPFC-p reach 25.7% and 25.6%, p = 0.675, no difference; with 1 to 5 s (Methods) 28.5% and 31.1%, p = 9.7e-09. Under both, every group is above 12.5% (p < 1e-100) and below untagged (41.9% and 49.0%). The criterion blocks the claim when the windows disagree.

outcomes.statement: In an early window (0 to 2 s) OB-p pseudo-populations decode odor identity better than mPFC-p pseudo-populations.
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 5; Figure 2I
outcomes.quote: we found that OB-p pseudo-populations outperformed mPFC-p pseudo-populations ( Figure 2I , two-sided Mann-Whitney U test with p = 2.15 × 10⁻ 30 )
outcomes.notes: OB-p 17.76%, mPFC-p 16.33%, untagged 25.09% in 0 to 2 s; OB-p against mPFC-p p = 5.0e-05 over 200 repeats. The difference (1.4 points) is far smaller than the paper's p = 2.15e-30 suggests.

outcomes.statement: With a sliding window, odor identity decoding accuracy peaks earlier for OB-p than for mPFC-p pseudo-populations.
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 5; Figure 2J
outcomes.quote: SVM classification using a sliding window for odor responses revealed that decoding accuracy for OB-p neurons peaked earlier than for mPFC-p neurons
outcomes.notes: The mean curve peaks at 5.75 s for OB-p and 9.25 s for mPFC-p with 250 ms windows, and at 5.50 and 9.00 s with 500 ms windows. The per-repeat peak times overlap widely (250 ms: OB-p 3.87 to 7.00 s, mPFC-p 2.12 to 12.17 s; medians 5.75 and 7.62 s), so the mPFC-p peak time is poorly determined, and the outcome may not hold under other seeds. Untagged peaks earliest (2.50 and 3.50 s). Before onset all groups are at or below chance (9.3 to 12.0%).
deviations: At 4.51 Hz a 250 ms window holds one frame; the windows are non-overlapping and start every 250 or 500 ms.

outcomes.statement: Late in the trial, mPFC-p pseudo-populations keep low but above-chance identity decoding that exceeds OB-p decoding.
outcomes.source: Results, OB-p and mPFC-p neurons exhibit broadly similar odor response properties, but differ in dynamics, paragraph 5; Figure 2K
outcomes.quote: mPFC-p pseudo-populations maintained low but above-chance identity decoding that exceeded OB-p decoding later in the trial
outcomes.notes: Late in the trial mPFC-p reaches 31.9 to 33.0% under the four combinations, above 12.5% (p <= 1.7e-88) and above OB-p (30.8 to 31.0%, p <= 3.8e-05). The differences are 1.2 to 2.1 points, and untagged is higher than both (38.8 to 41.7%).

outcomes.statement: Similar fractions of OB-p and mPFC-p neurons are tuned to odor identity, but OB-p neurons more often show significant effects of concentration and identity by concentration interactions, which are rare in mPFC-p neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Odor concentration is robustly encoded in OB-p but not mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 3B and 3C
outcomes.quote: Across time, similar fractions of OB-p and mPFC-p neurons were significantly tuned to odor identity ( Figure 3B ) ... By contrast, OB-p neurons were more likely to show significant main effects of concentration, as well as identity × concentration interactions
outcomes.notes: 0 to 5 s: identity 17.2% (OB-p) and 15.7% (mPFC-p), concentration 10.3% and 6.9%, interaction 9.2% and 6.9%. OB-p exceeds mPFC-p for concentration and interaction, and the identity difference (1.6 points) is smaller than the concentration difference (3.5). The time course shows OB-p higher for concentration mainly 1.5 to 4.5 s after onset; over 0 to 15 s the means are close (10.3 and 9.5%, 500 ms windows). The mPFC-p concentration and interaction fractions (6.9%) are near the 5% false positive level; its identity fraction (15.7%) is not. Untagged neurons have the highest fractions (22.2, 11.3 and 10.5%).
deviations: Type II sums of squares; the paper does not say which type (the design is nearly balanced, 9 or 10 trials per stimulus).
The time-resolved windows are non-overlapping, 500 ms and 1 s, from 2 s before onset.

outcomes.statement: OB-p pseudo-populations decode odor concentration more accurately and earlier than mPFC-p and untagged pseudo-populations, while mPFC-p decoding stays close to chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Odor concentration is robustly encoded in OB-p but not mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 3D and 3E
outcomes.quote: OB-p pseudo-populations reached higher concentration classification accuracy and did so earlier in the trial than both mPFC-p and untagged pseudo-populations, whereas mPFC-p ensembles supported only weak concentration decoding that remained close to chance
outcomes.notes: OB-p peaks highest (61.9% with 250 ms windows, 62.0% with 500 ms) and earliest (3.75 and 3.50 s), ahead of untagged (55.7% at 4.75 s; 54.0% at 4.50 s) and mPFC-p (53.6% at 9.75 s; 52.4% at 9.50 s). mPFC-p is not close to chance by the criterion's bound: its peak exceeds the midpoint between chance and the OB-p peak (47.6%) under both window readings, so the criterion's third condition fails. A peak chosen on half the repeats and read on the other half gives mPFC-p 53.56 and 51.84% (OB-p 61.91 and 61.96%), so the bias of taking a maximum does not change this. With concentration labels shuffled the accuracy is 32.1 to 35.2% (95th percentile 41.4 to 43.1%), so chance is 33.3% for this procedure. Before onset mPFC-p already decodes concentration at 37.2 to 37.6%, and trial order is not correlated with concentration in any session (|Spearman rho| <= 0.02); this offset is not explained. The first record gave partially reproduced; the verifier's not reproduced is adopted, since the criterion has no partial outcome and one of its three conditions fails.
deviations: Windows from 2 s before to 15 s after onset.

outcomes.statement: Pairwise concentration decoding (low against medium, medium against high, low against high) is strongest and most sustained in OB-p ensembles, intermediate in untagged neurons and weakest in mPFC-p neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Odor concentration is robustly encoded in OB-p but not mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 3; Figure S5G
outcomes.quote: concentration decoding was again strongest and most sustained in OB-p ensembles, intermediate in untagged neurons, and weakest in mPFC-p neurons
outcomes.notes: The order OB-p > untagged > mPFC-p holds only for 0.1% against 1% (OB-p 62.3 and 62.4%, untagged 62.1 and 61.4%, mPFC-p 56.2 and 56.7%). For 1% against 10% and 0.1% against 10% the three groups are within 2.2 points of each other and untagged is highest under both window readings.

outcomes.statement: Across the three concentrations, response sparseness and the fraction of active cells change only modestly in all three populations.
outcomes.source: Results, Odor concentration is robustly encoded in OB-p but not mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 2; Figure S5A to S5D
outcomes.quote: overall response sparseness and the fraction of active cells changed only modestly in all three populations ( Figure S5 )
outcomes.notes: No population shows a monotonic change of more than half its 0.1% value, under either window reading. The largest change is the untagged percentage of active cells, 7.3% to 10.8% (+47.9%, start) and 7.1% to 10.6% (+48.1%, centre); OB-p active cells rise by 34% and 37%; lifetime and population sparseness change by 12% or less. The judgement rests on the criterion's reading of 'only modestly'.
deviations: Population sparseness per subject is computed per trial over the subject's cells of the group and averaged over trials; the Figure S5D legend gives no more detail.

outcomes.statement: Go/NoGo performance improves across training days, with no difference between OB- p and mPFC-p labelled mice, reaching 73.7% correct trials on day 3.
outcomes.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: Behavioral performance improved as training progressed, with no significant difference between OB-p and mPFC-p labelled mice ... with, on average, 73.7% correct trials (hit and correct rejection) on day 3
outcomes.notes: With 7 mice the day 3 mean is 76.9% (hits as scored) and 76.4% (relabeled), within tolerance, and the day means rise (69.6, 72.5, 76.9%). The day effect is not significant: repeated-measures F = 1.571 (p = 0.248) and 2.452 (p = 0.128), against F = 4.375, and mixed-ANOVA day p = 0.246 and 0.118. Projection (p = 0.66) and interaction (p >= 0.26) are not significant, as in the paper. With all 8 mice and relabeled hits F = 3.742 (p = 0.0499), still outside tolerance, with mixed-ANOVA day p = 0.029. The NWB outcome labels do not apply the 10 s relabeling: it changes 0 to 3 trials per session.
deviations: The paper's Go/NoGo experiment has 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p); the dandiset has 8. The analysis leaves out sub-668, an assumption: it is the only Go/NoGo mouse without tracking identifiers and has 24 to 58 cells per session against 98 to 361 for the others. Its day 3 performance (90%) passes the Methods' 60% exclusion threshold, so the paper's stated rule does not exclude it. The outcome is the same with all 8 mice.

outcomes.statement: Anticipatory licking in response to the rewarded odorants increases across training.
outcomes.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 2; Figure 4C right and Figure S6
outcomes.quote: an increase in anticipatory licking in response to the rewarded odorants
outcomes.notes: With 7 mice the mean CS+ lick rate 2 to 5 s after onset is 0.49, 1.07 and 1.90 licks/s on days 1 to 3, and 0.50, 0.99 and 1.68 over 0 to 5 s. Each of the 8 mice licks more on day 3 than on day 1 under both readings.

outcomes.statement: In expert mice (day 3), OB-p pseudo-populations decode odor identity above chance in all four task phases, peaking early (delay) and declining later, whereas mPFC-p pseudo-populations are near chance early and improve later in the trial.
outcomes.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 4D, 4E and 4F
outcomes.quote: odor identity decoding in OB-p pseudo-populations was greater than chance across all 4 task phases ... Decoding accuracy peaked during early trial phases (delay phase after odor exposure), but declined later in the trial (action) ... In contrast, mPFC-p pseudo-populations performed near chance during early trial phases, but decoding accuracy increased later in the trial
outcomes.notes: 7 mice, mean aggregate: OB-p 54.5, 75.0, 71.0 and 58.6% in odor, delay, act-early and act-late, above 25% in every phase (corrected p <= 5e-71), highest in the delay and lower in act-late; mPFC-p 36.4, 52.7, 65.8 and 60.2%, lowest in odor and delay, highest in act-early. The maximum aggregate and all 8 mice give the same pattern. mPFC-p is above chance in every phase (odor corrected p = 5e-43), so 'near chance' holds only as lowest against 25%. With labels shuffled this procedure gives 26 to 29% (95th percentile 36 to 39%), a little above 25%. Every mean is higher than the shuffled means, but mPFC-p odor (36.4% with 7 mice and the mean aggregate, 36.2 and 36.1% with 8) is below the mPFC-p shuffled 95th percentile (37.2 and 37.1%); only 7 mice with the maximum (37.3%) is just above it. OB-p exceeds mPFC-p in odor, delay and act-early (corrected p <= 3.1e-12), not in act-late (p = 0.12). By mouse, from its own red cells, each of the three mPFC mice decodes least in the odor phase (sub-2456 31.4%, sub-2457 30.0%, sub-644 35.5%), so the pattern is not carried by sub-2456 and sub-2457 alone (61 of the 93 day 3 mPFC-p cells). In the per-session clock check these two mice decode CS identity later and less early in the trial (34 to 51% in 1 to 2 s after onset, against 56 to 85% for the other mice except sub-2400 day 1, 40%); later sub-2456 reaches 73 to 74% on days 2 and 3, above any sub-2400 session (at most 70%), while sub-2457 stays at or below 63%. The onset frame equals the files' stim_onset_frame in every trial. Before onset the per-session accuracies are 20 to 39%; no per-session null was run, and some sessions sit above the pooled tables' shuffled means of 26 to 29% (sub-664 day 3 at 34 to 37%, sub-2456 day 2 at 32 to 39%). The day 3 mean traces of sub-2457, sub-2400 and sub-2401 drift upward before onset (sub-2457 0.80 at frame -4, 0.85 at frame 0) and keep rising after it. This is consistent with a shared clock and slower or weaker odor responses, not a proof of it. The 30 Hz passive data, aligned to sniffs independently, also show these two mice to be slow, untagged cells included (fig2f-latency).
deviations: The paper's Go/NoGo experiment has 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p); the dandiset has 8. The analysis leaves out sub-668, an assumption: it is the only Go/NoGo mouse without tracking identifiers and has 24 to 58 cells per session against 98 to 361 for the others. Its day 3 performance (90%) passes the Methods' 60% exclusion threshold, so the paper's stated rule does not exclude it. The outcome is the same with all 8 mice.
Trials are matched across mice by CS and order and truncated to the smallest count: 70 trials on day 3, with 9 for the least frequent CS.

outcomes.statement: Generalized odor valence can be decoded above chance from a general PCx (any-p) pseudo-population in all task phases in expert mice.
outcomes.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 4; Figure 4G and Figure S8H
outcomes.quote: We found that odor valence could be decoded with high accuracy from a general PCx pseudo-population across all phases
outcomes.notes: Any-p generalized valence: 54.1, 69.3, 64.5 and 60.2% (7 mice, mean aggregate), all above 50% (corrected p <= 9.1e-07); the maximum aggregate and all 8 mice also give p < 0.05 in every phase.
deviations: The paper's Go/NoGo experiment has 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p); the dandiset has 8. The analysis leaves out sub-668, an assumption: it is the only Go/NoGo mouse without tracking identifiers and has 24 to 58 cells per session against 98 to 361 for the others. Its day 3 performance (90%) passes the Methods' 60% exclusion threshold, so the paper's stated rule does not exclude it. The outcome is the same with all 8 mice.

outcomes.statement: In expert mice OB-p pseudo-populations encode generalized valence in the odor and delay phases but fall to chance in the action phases, while mPFC-p pseudo-populations encode valence in the later but not the earliest phase; the two differ in all four phases.
outcomes.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 5; Figure 4H
outcomes.quote: OB-p pseudo-populations accurately encoded odor valence during early phases of the trial (odor exposure, delay), but that decoding accuracy decreased to chance level later in the trial (action) ... In contrast, mPFC-p pseudo-populations encoded odor valence during later but not early phases of the trial
outcomes.notes: 7 mice, mean aggregate: OB-p 62.6, 66.9, 47.7 and 56.2%, above 50% in odor and delay, at chance in act-early (corrected p = 1.0) and above chance in act-late (p = 1.7e-25), where the claim has it at chance. mPFC-p 52.0, 60.1, 59.8 and 64.2%, above chance in delay and both action phases and also in odor (p = 4.1e-10). Under the maximum mPFC-p is at chance in odor (49.4%, p = 1.0) but OB-p is still above chance in act-late (56.7%, p = 4.7e-26). OB-p and mPFC-p differ in all four phases under both aggregates. The paper's text has OB-p above chance in act-early (p = 0.00141) and at chance in act-late (p = 1); here it is the reverse.
deviations: The paper's Go/NoGo experiment has 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p); the dandiset has 8. The analysis leaves out sub-668, an assumption: it is the only Go/NoGo mouse without tracking identifiers and has 24 to 58 cells per session against 98 to 361 for the others. Its day 3 performance (90%) passes the Methods' 60% exclusion threshold, so the paper's stated rule does not exclude it. The outcome is the same with all 8 mice.

outcomes.statement: Restricted to correct trials, OB-p pseudo-populations encode valence well early and much less later, mPFC-p pseudo-populations encode it more accurately late than early, and the two differ in all four phases.
outcomes.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraphs 6 and 7; Figure 4I and 4J
outcomes.quote: OB-p pseudo-populations accurately encoded odor valence during early phases of the trial but much less so later ... mPFC-p pseudo-populations encoded odor valence late in correct trials more accurately than early ... For all four task phases, these projection pseudo-populations performed differently from one another at decoding valence for correct trials
outcomes.notes: Neither correct-trial table is credibly the paper's, and the claim's pass depends on which one is used. On the table matched as for all trials (30 trials, 17, 6, 4 and 3 per CS, 77% CS+) shuffled labels give 65.5 to 69.0%, not the paper's 50%; under it OB-p reaches 83.5, 83.7, 79.4 and 81.9% and mPFC-p 72.6, 80.7, 80.4 and 82.7% (mean aggregate), mPFC-p odor is above 50% and the groups differ in 2 or 3 of 4 phases, which would not reproduce the claim. The first record gave not reproduced on that table. On the table balanced over the 4 CS (3 correct pseudo-trials each, 12 in all, 7 mice, shuffled level 42 to 51%), with the maximum aggregate, OB-p reaches 78.9, 70.4, 55.8 and 55.2% in odor, delay, act-early and act-late, higher early than in both action phases; mPFC-p 31.4, 47.3, 66.5 and 86.8%, higher in both action phases, not above 50% in odor (corrected p = 1); OB-p and mPFC-p differ in all 4 phases (corrected p <= 1.6e-12). With the mean aggregate all holds but the act-early difference (p = 1). On the balanced table mPFC-p reaches 27.8% (mean) and 31.4% (maximum) in the odor phase, about 20 points below that table's mean shuffled level (51.3 and 51.0%); only 6% and 12% of shuffled repeats fall below these accuracies (Mann-Whitney p = 3e-14 and 1.4e-11), so the decoder predicts systematically below its null and this does not show mPFC-p at chance. The shuffled repeats spread from about 15 to 82% (5th to 95th percentiles). The paper reports a correct-trial valence scheme in the stability analysis across days (Figure 5F); matched by CS and order, day 1 has only 1 correct trial per CS, so the paper's correct-trial pseudo-populations were probably not built by CS-order matching at all. A class-weighted decoder or balanced accuracy on the matched table would put chance near 50% while keeping the matching, but the paper does not describe it. The paper's construction cannot be identified, so the claim is blocked as methods_underspecified after the third verification round.
deviations: The paper's Go/NoGo experiment has 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p); the dandiset has 8. The analysis leaves out sub-668, an assumption: it is the only Go/NoGo mouse without tracking identifiers and has 24 to 58 cells per session against 98 to 361 for the others. Its day 3 performance (90%) passes the Methods' 60% exclusion threshold, so the paper's stated rule does not exclude it. The outcome is the same with all 8 mice.
Correct trials are matched across mice by CS and by order among that mouse's correct trials of the CS, the Methods' matching rule applied to the subset.

Assumed that the correct-trial pseudo-populations are balanced over the 4 CS, each truncated to the smallest CS count (3). The paper states chance at 50% for these panels and excludes days 1 and 2 "due to imbalanced counts of correct trials across animals to properly construct pseudo-populations" (Figure 4I-J legend); the matched but unbalanced table has a chance level near 66%. The question is recorded for the paper's authors.

outcomes.statement: Generalized valence decoding in correct trials differs between OB-p and mPFC-p pseudo-populations in the odor and act-early phases but not in the delay and act-late phases.
outcomes.source: Results, Differential encoding of odor valence in OB-p and mPFC-p neurons, paragraph 7; Figure S8E, S8G and S8K
outcomes.quote: We also observed significant differences with generalized valence decoding performance in correct trials between projection pseudo-populations during odor and act-early phases
outcomes.notes: OB-p and mPFC-p differ in odor (corrected p = 4.3e-33) as claimed, but also in delay (p = 2.5e-33, mPFC-p higher by 9.1 points) and act-late (p = 0.018); act-early differs under the mean aggregate (p = 1.5e-06) and not under the maximum (p = 0.18). The pattern holds under no reading, with 7 or 8 mice. That table's shuffled-label level is 61 to 64%, not 50%. On the table balanced over the 4 CS (3 correct trials each, shuffled level 46 to 51%, the reading of fig4ij-valence-correct-trials) all four phases differ (corrected p <= 6e-05 mean, <= 1.9e-07 maximum), so the outcome is the same under both tables.
deviations: The paper's Go/NoGo experiment has 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p); the dandiset has 8. The analysis leaves out sub-668, an assumption: it is the only Go/NoGo mouse without tracking identifiers and has 24 to 58 cells per session against 98 to 361 for the others. Its day 3 performance (90%) passes the Methods' 60% exclusion threshold, so the paper's stated rule does not exclude it. The outcome is the same with all 8 mice.

outcomes.statement: The differences in timing of identity and valence encoding between OB-p and mPFC- p ensembles increase over the course of learning.
outcomes.source: Discussion, Functional specializations of projection neurons align with those of their target areas, paragraph 1; Figure S7A and Figure S9
outcomes.quote: Notably, these differences increased over the course of learning
outcomes.notes: Identity, mean aggregate: OB-p accuracy rises over days in odor (median slope 8.0 points per day) and delay (8.5), mPFC-p in act-early (13.7) and act-late (9.4), all above the day-shuffled null (corrected p < 0.05). The same holds for identity with the maximum and for generalized valence with the mean, not for generalized valence with the maximum. Both groups also rise in most other phases (mPFC-p identity in odor 2.0 and delay 5.2), so the criterion's test shows accuracy growing in the named phases, not the OB-p and mPFC-p difference itself growing. With 1000 slopes against 1000 null slopes, the Mann-Whitney test is significant for almost any shift. The difference itself (OB-p minus mPFC-p, identity, mean aggregate) grows from day 1 to day 3 in odor (5.0, 14.3, 18.0 points) and delay (15.0, 10.9, 22.2) and shrinks in act-early (29.5, -3.2, 5.7) and act-late (23.1, -1.4, -1.6). Whether the criterion reads the statement as the paper means is asked of a reader (questions/daste-2025.yaml).
deviations: The paper's Go/NoGo experiment has 7 mice (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p); the dandiset has 8. The analysis leaves out sub-668, an assumption: it is the only Go/NoGo mouse without tracking identifiers and has 24 to 58 cells per session against 98 to 361 for the others. Its day 3 performance (90%) passes the Methods' 60% exclusion threshold, so the paper's stated rule does not exclude it. Only the 7-mouse analysis was run for this claim.

outcomes.statement: Longitudinal tracking across the three Go/NoGo sessions follows 46 OB-p and 41 mPFC-p neurons in 4 OB-p and 3 mPFC-p tagged mice.
outcomes.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 1; Methods, Longitudinal tracking
outcomes.quote: we longitudinally tracked identified neurons across three Go/NoGo sessions and followed 46 OB-p and 41 mPFC-p neurons in 4 OB-p–tagged and 3 mPFC-p–tagged mice
outcomes.notes: The code's criterion (identifier present on days 0 to 3, red in at least 3 sessions) gives exactly 46 OB-p and 41 mPFC-p neurons. They come from 3 OB-p mice (sub-2400 20, sub-2401 16, sub-513 10; sub-664 none) and 3 mPFC-p mice (sub-2457 19, sub-2456 13, sub-644 9), not the 4 OB-p mice the statement names. Other criteria give 73 and 64, 35 and 30, 26 and 20. The code counts red sessions over all sessions, which includes day 4 of GNG_2023b; counted over days 0 to 3 only, as the claims file words it, the counts are 43 and 37, also within tolerance.

outcomes.statement: Tracked OB-p and mPFC-p neurons do not differ in the average slope of their session-averaged normalized fluorescence across the three Go/NoGo days.
outcomes.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 2; Figure S10D
outcomes.quote: there was no significant difference in the average slope between OB-p and mPFC-p neurons

statistics.about: combination of valence and task phase

outcomes.notes: Mixed ANOVA on slopes: projection F = 0.88, p = 0.35 (paper 0.36); combination p = 0.043 (paper 0.11); interaction p = 0.0035 (paper 0.0031). Mean slopes -0.006 (OB-p) and 0.008 (mPFC-p) per day. Tracked neurons come from 3 OB-p and 3 mPFC-p mice; per mouse mean slopes range -0.024 to 0.049.

outcomes.statement: Changes in lifetime sparseness across sessions show no clear effect of projection target.
outcomes.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 2; Figure S10E
outcomes.quote: We similarly quantified changes in lifetime sparseness across sessions and did not observe a clear effect of projection target
outcomes.notes: Most tracked neurons are never active in some phase on some day, which leaves their sparseness undefined. Leaving those neurons out: projection p = 0.29 (start reading, 16 of 87 neurons kept) and 0.48 (centre, 8 kept). With all 87 neurons and undefined sparseness set to 1: p = 0.38 and 0.45; set to 0: p = 0.082 and 0.048. Only the last variant finds a projection effect. The paper's phase effect (p = 0.0491) is not found under the main readings (p = 0.13 and 0.82). The test has little power. The OB-p minus mPFC-p difference of mean slope is +0.032 per day, 95% interval -0.022 to +0.087 (start, 16 neurons; SD of neuron slopes 0.058), and +0.014 (-0.018 to +0.046) with all 87 neurons and undefined values set to 1, so differences of several hundredths per day are not excluded; the absence holds only in the sense of the criterion.
deviations: How neurons without a defined lifetime sparseness enter the test is not stated. Assumed that they are left out, the standard treatment of an undefined value; this keeps only 16 or 8 of 87 neurons, and the variants that keep all neurons are shown. The question is recorded for the paper's authors.

outcomes.statement: Tracked OB-p neurons show a higher coefficient of variation of session-averaged fluorescence across days than mPFC-p neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 3; Figure 5C
outcomes.quote: OB-p neurons typically showed higher fluorescence CV across days than mPFC-p neurons ( Figure 5C, D ). A mixed ANOVA on CV within combinations of odors and task phases revealed a significant effect of projection target (p = 0.0127)
outcomes.notes: Under odor (CS) by phase, 16 levels, the projection effect has p = 0.0115 (paper 0.0127) with the OB-p median CV higher (0.230 against 0.193); the combination effect p = 0.012 (paper 0.037) and the interaction p = 0.46 (paper 0.43). All 1392 session-averaged means are positive (0.198 to 1.677), so the two CV readings give identical values. Each of the 3 OB-p mice has a higher median CV (0.223 to 0.265) than each of the 3 mPFC-p mice (0.187 to 0.212). No per-condition Mann-Whitney test survives Benjamini-Hochberg correction (0 of 16), as in Figure S10F. What the answer changed: the first run blocked the claim as methods_underspecified, because the criterion then also required the valence by phase reading, which gives projection p = 0.067 (OB-p median 0.162 against 0.145). The reader answered (questions/000785.yaml) that the paper names odor by phase for this test and amended the criterion to use it alone, with valence by phase as a variant only; the computation is unchanged, and under the amended criterion the claim is reproduced.
deviations: The CV uses the SD with ddof 0 (a standard choice). Ranking ('matched-ranked' neurons) is not applied; the criterion runs the ANOVA on raw CVs.

outcomes.statement: Identity decoding transfers across sessions comparably in tracked OB-p and mPFC-p ensembles, whereas generalized valence decoding transfers better in mPFC-p ensembles, especially across distal sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 4; Figure 5E and Figure S11
outcomes.quote: When decoding odor identity, transferability across dissimilar sessions was comparable between OB-p and mPFC-p ensembles ... whereas mPFC-p ensembles maintained higher valence decoding accuracy, particularly for generalized valence across distal sessions
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), every qualifying entry: identity does not differ for proximal (OB-p 30.0%, mPFC-p 30.2%, corrected p = 1.0) or distal sessions (31.1 against 30.0%, p = 1.0); distal generalized valence is higher for mPFC-p (55.9 against 48.3%, corrected p < 0.0001); the maximum aggregate gives the same. Reading (b), per-mouse means with 3 mice per group, cannot reach significance (smallest corrected p = 0.6). Within session, OB-p identity is higher under the maximum (37.1 against 32.7%, p = 0.0005), in the direction of the paper's within-session result. Entries are not independent (they share mice, neurons and trials), which inflates the significance of reading (a). Leaving out one mouse at a time under reading (a), distal generalized valence stays higher for mPFC-p (corrected p <= 0.0019 under both aggregates). The identity part fails without sub-2400 (OB-p higher for distal sessions, corrected p = 0.0062 mean and 0.00015 maximum aggregate) and, under the maximum, without sub-2456 (p = 0.041), so it holds in 5 of the 6 leave-one-out sets under the mean aggregate and in 4 of 6 under the maximum.
deviations: Within a session, train and test trials are split by stratified 5-fold cross-validation, the claims file's reading; across sessions all trials of one day train and all of the other test.

outcomes.statement: The temporal structure of valence coding across sessions is more stable in tracked mPFC-p than OB-p ensembles, while odor identity coding is not.
outcomes.source: Results, Longitudinal tracking reveals greater stability of valence encoding in feedforward projection neurons, paragraph 5; Figure 5F and Figure S12B
outcomes.quote: These analyses revealed that the temporal structure of valence coding was consistently more stable in mPFC-p than in OB-p ensembles
outcomes.notes: No combination of readings has all three valence schemes differ, which the criterion requires. With all block pairs, every correlation as a sample and the maximum aggregate, mPFC-p is more stable for generalized valence (r 0.31 against 0.15, corrected p = 0.0015) and correct-trial valence (0.30 against 0.12, p = 0.0014), but not for valence (0.35 against 0.29, p = 0.13); identity does not differ (p = 1.0). mPFC-p has the higher mean correlation in 22 of 24 valence comparisons. With per-mouse means no test is significant. The first record gave partially reproduced; the verifier's not reproduced is adopted, since the criterion has no partial outcome.

findings.statement: The imaging rate stated in the ImagingPlane metadata is wrong in 21 files: 30 Hz (concentration session of sub-2400) and 50 or 100 Hz (all GNG_2023b sessions) where the plane timestamps give 4.51 to 4.52 Hz per plane.

The Go/NoGo experiment holds 8 mice, 4 OB-tagged and 4 mPFC-tagged, where the paper has 7 (4 OB-p, 3 mPFC-p). The extra mPFC mouse is presumably sub-668, the only one without tracking identifiers, with 24 to 58 cells per session; its day 3 performance (90% correct) passes the paper's exclusion threshold of 60%, and nothing in the dandiset says why it is left out.

The paper's counts are matched only when planes without red cells are left out, as the paper's code does; over all planes the identity experiment has 2328 untagged neurons, against 1937 with the rule and 1978 in the paper. In sub-164 and sub-8 the plane without red cells nearly repeats plane 0 (mean-image r = 0.994 and 0.996), consistent with the code's comment about duplicated planes. The files do not mark these planes.

Four identity sessions (sub-8, sub-9, sub-163, sub-164, recorded in 2020) have 80 trials of 30 s with odor onset about 10 s into the trial, while the other six have 100 trials of 22 s with onset at 5.1 s; the paper describes 22 s trials with a 5 s baseline.
Under the paper code's criterion, the 46 tracked OB-p neurons come from 3 OB-p mice (sub-664 contributes none), not 4.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The executed notebooks of the first run (passive and Go/NoGo) with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier checked the archive's assets through the DANDI API for the blocked claims and tested mwu_greater_p, vinje_gallant, mutual_info_bits, the notebook's anova2, pseudo_population, hit_relabel and binarize on synthetic inputs. Its outcomes agree with the record as it then stood on 34 of 36 claims; it gave not reproduced where the record had partially reproduced for fig3de-concentration-decoding and fig5f-stability. It reported no place where the claims file misreads the paper; its point 8, that the criterion of discussion-differences-grow does not test whether the difference grows, is asked of a reader in questions/daste-2025.yaml. Its point 10 (np.clip in load_session) is answered by a count the notebooks now print, 0 clipped trial windows in every experiment (920 identity, 1000 concentration, 500 at 30 Hz and 3220 Go/NoGo trials); its point 11 (helper tests) needed no change. Report in transcripts/daste-2025/verifier-1-report.md.

disagreements.reason: mPFC-p peaks at 53.6% and 52.4%, above the midpoints of 47.6% and 47.7%. Problem 7, mPFC-p decoding before onset is 37.2-37.6% against a 33.3% chance with near-balanced classes, unexplained, and the peak of the mean curve across about 68 windows is biased upward by taking a maximum; mPFC-p fails the midpoint by about 6 points either way.
No combination of readings meets the criterion. Unconstrained valence is never significant.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebooks of the author-revise-1 run (passive and Go/NoGo), the helper module, the entry README, the claims file and the attempt record, with the paper. The verifier agreed with 34 of the 36 outcomes; it would give blocked (methods_underspecified) for fig4ij-valence-correct-trials and, agreeing only in part, for fig2b-lifetime-sparseness-similar. It found no new place where the claims file misreads the paper. In reply both outcomes are kept as verified and a change to blocked is proposed on each, for a third round; the sentences it found unsupported are corrected in the notebooks, the record and the README, and the notebooks now print the claim's condition under each treatment of never-active neurons (fig2b), the balanced correct-trial accuracies against their shuffled repeats (fig4ij), and the latencies of projection neurons against their own mouse's untagged neurons (fig2f). Report in transcripts/daste-2025/verifier-2-report.md.

disagreements.reason: Agrees only partly. The assumption (never-active neurons left out) is stated, but the criterion fixes n at 81/84/1978, every neuron, which argues for keeping them. The two readings that keep every neuron disagree, set to 0 the claim is reproduced (smallest corrected p 0.061), set to 1 it is not. The data therefore do not settle the outcome; it would record methods_underspecified, and if the outcome stays it should stay marked as assumed.

Disagrees; it would give blocked (methods_underspecified). The assumption (correct-trial tables balanced to 3 trials per CS) is stated but not well supported. The Methods also decode "odor identity for correct trials" on the 4 CS, which the notebook says cannot be cross-validated with 3 trials per CS, so the paper's table was probably not a 3-per-CS table. The matched table's shuffled level is 65-69%, against the paper's 50%. Under the balanced reading the claim passes only with the maximum aggregate; with the mean, act-early fails (p = 1). The condition "mPFC-p odor not above 50%" is met by 27.8% and 31.4%, about 20 points below that table's shuffled level of about 51%; a 12-trial decoder that systematically anti-predicts is misbehaving and does not show mPFC-p at chance, and the notes do not mention it. Neither table is credibly the paper's procedure.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 3. The two proposed changes of outcome, on fig2b-lifetime-sparseness-similar and fig4ij-valence-correct-trials, with the analysis behind them in the full executed notebooks of the author-revise-2 run, the attempt record and the claims file. Nothing else was reviewed. The verifier agreed with both proposals and found no place where the claims file misreads the paper. Both outcomes are now blocked (methods_underspecified). Report in transcripts/daste-2025/verifier-3-report.md.

paper_notes.statement: The Methods count 18 mice as 9 OB-p and 8 mPFC-p, and the Figure S2B legend has 9 OB-p and 10 mPFC-p mice; the dandiset has 18 subjects, 10 OB-tagged and 8 mPFC-tagged.

The transformer and MLP hyperparameters and the held-out animal pairs (Tables 5, 6 and 8) are missing from the preprint's text, and the figure analysis code is not yet released, so the projection-classifier claims cannot be run. Question for the authors: can Tables 2 to 8 and the analysis code be released?

Question for the authors: how many comparisons does the Bonferroni correction of Figure 2E cover? With the 3 group pairs the unreliable-cell difference is not significant under any reading tried here; with the 2 tests it is under one (baseline over the 5 s before onset, per-trial baseline, reliability over all odor trials, each mouse's own trials).

Question for the authors: how do neurons without a defined lifetime sparseness (never active in a phase on a day) enter the slope analysis of Figure S10E and the comparison of Figure 2B? Leaving them out keeps 16 of 87 tracked neurons; setting their sparseness to 0 or 1 keeps all and changes the projection p-value from 0.29 to 0.08 or 0.38. For Figure 2B the two values give different outcomes (set to 0, no pair differs; set to 1, OB-p and mPFC-p each differ from untagged).

Question for the authors: which mice form the Go/NoGo dataset, and is sub-668 excluded? The analyses here assume it is. Also, is the 0.7 s window of the response binarization placed at the start of each frame or centred on it? Both readings were run and give the same outcomes here.

Question for the authors: how were the correct-trial pseudo-populations of Figures 4I-J and S8E-G built? Matched by CS and order across the 7 mice, day 3 keeps 17, 6, 4 and 3 correct trials per CS (77% CS+), and shuffled labels then give 65 to 69% for valence, not the stated 50%. Balancing each CS to 3 trials gives a chance near 50% but only 12 trials, and on it mPFC-p odor-phase valence decoding falls about 20 points below the shuffled level. Matched by CS and order, day 1 has only 1 correct trial per CS, which the correct-trial scheme of Figure 5F would need. Figures 4I-J are blocked here as methods underspecified.

entries.name: daste-2025
entries.title: Projection-specific routing of odor information in the olfactory cortex (Daste, Pierré et al. 2025)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Daste, Pierré et al. (2025) on dandiset 000785, which holds two-photon imaging of OB-projecting and mPFC-projecting neurons in anterior piriform cortex during passive odor exposure (identity, concentration and 30 Hz experiments) and Go/NoGo learning, with cells tracked across sessions. It covers the neuron counts, single-cell response properties, odor identity and concentration decoding, behavior, valence decoding and the tracked-neuron analyses.
